business.name: Northgate Lettings
business.industry: Residential letting agency and block management
business.notes: Two directors, three property managers, one lettings negotiator, one accounts person, and two part time weekend viewing staff. They manage 412 tenancies. Reapit is the system of record but the property managers keep their own Excel trackers because they say Reapit reporting is unusable. One director thinks everything is in Reapit. It is not.

processes.name: Triaging tenant maintenance reports
processes.description: Tenants report faults by phone, by email to the shared mailbox, through the tenant portal, and increasingly by texting whichever property manager they have a mobile number for. The property manager reads the report and decides whether it is an emergency, whether it is the landlord's responsibility or the tenant's, and which contractor to send. If it needs landlord approval because it is over the agreed limit, she emails the landlord and waits, sometimes for days. Once approved she calls or emails the contractor, then updates the job in Reapit, then emails the tenant to say someone is coming. She chases the contractor if she has not heard back within a week.
processes.pain_description: This is what the property managers say ruins their week. Reports arrive through five channels so things get missed, and two complaints went to the ombudsman last year over repairs that were reported and never actioned, one of which cost them a landlord with six properties. Tenants ring to chase because they never hear anything back. The property managers say they spend more time telling people what is happening than making anything happen. One of them left in March and said this was why.
processes.baseline_metric: open maintenance jobs showing in Reapit, usually around 60 at any time
processes.data_notes: Reports arrive as free text in email, as voice notes, as texts on personal phones, and as portal submissions which are structured. Reapit holds the tenancy and property records properly. The portal is used by maybe a fifth of tenants.

processes.name: Chasing rent arrears
processes.description: Rent is due on various dates depending on the tenancy. Each morning the accounts person opens the bank feed in Sage, matches payments against expected rent in a spreadsheet exported from Reapit, and marks off what has landed. She then works through the unmatched list, sends a first reminder email from a saved template, and notes the date in her spreadsheet. If nothing arrives after five days she sends a second letter, and after fourteen days she passes it to the property manager, who calls the tenant and emails the landlord to let them know.
processes.pain_description: The matching is fiddly because tenants pay from accounts in different names, pay part amounts, or pay two months at once. About thirty payments a month need manual investigation. The reminder emails go out late whenever the accounts person is off, and nobody covers it properly. Arrears crept up over the winter and the directors did not spot it until the quarterly landlord reports went out and three landlords complained.
processes.baseline_metric: arrears as a percentage of rent due, reported to landlords quarterly, currently 4.1 percent
processes.data_notes: Bank feed in Sage is structured and reliable. Expected rent comes out of Reapit as a CSV export, which the accounts person does by hand each morning. Her chase tracking lives in her own Excel file on her desktop.

processes.name: Processing tenant applications and referencing
processes.description: An applicant fills in a paper or PDF form, or sometimes just emails the details. The negotiator checks it is complete, chases whatever is missing, then keys the details into the referencing provider's portal and uploads the identity documents. The provider comes back in two to five days. If the reference is passed she drafts the tenancy agreement in Reapit and sends it out through DocuSign. If it is referred or failed she calls the applicant and discusses a guarantor, which starts the whole thing again for the guarantor.
processes.pain_description: Applications arrive incomplete nine times out of ten, so the negotiator spends her time chasing bank details and previous landlord contacts. Applicants get impatient and two walked to another agent in June because the process took eleven days. The identity documents come as phone photos that are often unreadable, and one was accepted last year that turned out to be altered, which the directors are still nervous about.
processes.data_notes: Application data arrives as PDFs, phone photos, and free text emails. The referencing portal has an API according to the provider, but nobody at Northgate has asked about it. Reapit holds the outcome.

processes.name: Producing monthly landlord statements
processes.description: On the tenth of each month the accounts person runs the client account report in Reapit, exports it to Excel, checks each landlord's deductions for management fees and any contractor invoices paid that month, corrects the ones that pulled through wrong, then generates the statements and emails them out. She sends about forty by post because those landlords have asked for paper.
processes.pain_description: It takes the best part of two days and the accounts person cannot do anything else while it runs. Roughly fifteen statements a month need a manual correction, usually because a contractor invoice was coded to the wrong property. Landlords query about five a month, which the director then has to unpick. It has never gone badly wrong but it eats the middle of every month.
processes.baseline_metric: statement queries raised by landlords, about five a month
processes.data_notes: Reapit holds the transactions in structured form and exports cleanly to Excel. Contractor invoices are coded by hand when they are entered, which is where the errors come from.

processes.name: Returning tenancy deposits
processes.description: At the end of a tenancy the property manager does a check out inspection against the inventory, takes photos on her phone, and writes up what she thinks should be deducted. She emails the proposal to the tenant and the landlord and waits for both to agree. If they agree she instructs the deposit scheme to release, and if they do not she prepares evidence for a dispute.
processes.pain_description: The waiting is the worst part, because a tenant who has moved out stops replying and the clock in the scheme rules keeps running. They lost two disputes last year because the check in inventory photos were too poor to prove anything. Property managers describe writing up a deduction proposal as the job they most put off.
processes.data_notes: Inventories are PDF reports from an inventory clerk. Check out photos are on personal phones and get uploaded inconsistently. The deposit scheme has a portal with no export that anyone knows of.
